Part I: Kn o wled g e Base  •  Part II: Q&A Pairs
Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 1 14, English)
Ashaeiynn Third-Eye Master class: Samarpan, Tap Shakti, Receptors, and the Path to a Mantra-Charged Body

This session's sour ce material arrived as several consecutive pieces with no fr esh opening gr eeting, sankalp, or "welcome to X" framing between them (one piece contains a passing, non-gr eeting r emark of "welcome to Ashaeiynn, guys" mid-explanation, not a session-opening addr ess), and the very first piece begins mid-conversation. All pieces ar e treated as one continuous session because they shar e the same r ecurring devotees as illustrative examples thr oughout (Anshu, her sister Shalini/Shalu, Vikas bhaiya, Shrikant bhaiya, Shivram bhaiya, Rohit bhaiya) and the same overar ching subject — an extended "thir d-eye" master class on what actually makes a devotee's inner vision (drishti) r eliable and safe: samarpan (surr ender), tap shakti (accumulated spiritual heat/power built thr ough sustained japa), the guru's own techniques for safely raising this ener gy , and the dangers of pursuing visible drishti without the underlying mantra shakti to support it. The material trails off mid-sentence at the end. Its overall topic (thir d-eye training, drishti, tap shakti) has no overlap with the immediately pr eceding session (Session 1 13's English-language "concept of master" dialogue), so this entir e body of material is tr eated as its own, separate session rather than a continuation of Session 1 13. The devotee names used her e ar e this teaching's own illustrative pedagogical examples, r eferenced dir ectly by the speaker as part of the teaching, and ar e pr eserved as such; sensitive personal history (e.g., a devotee's past "doshas") is described only in general terms, consistent with this pr oject's privacy practice. This document is Knowledge Base and Q&A only — the sour ce material's live back-and-forth exchanges ar e informal r emarks embedded within an extended monologue rather than sustained, independently quotable sangat dialogue, so no separate Hinglish curatedconversation section is included. Because this session describes r eal historical instances of tantrik attack (burning kriya) and defensive tap shakti, it must be tr eated strictly as this teaching's own descriptive, pr otective, devotional framework — never as instructions for attempting either technique on a r eal person.
Part A — Even Krishna and Bholenath Rely on Being "T old": Why No One Sees Pur ely on Their Own

1. The starting r eminder — don't over -rely on your own mind, keep samarpan: Per this teaching, someone overthinking a situation with their own mind is advised instead to hold samarpan (surrender/trust) — reassured that "someone will come and tell you" rather than needing to work it out through their own thinking.

2. Even Bhagwan Krishna does not simply "know" everything by sitting still, per this teaching: Per this teaching, despite being described as the Lord of all three lokas (worlds), even Bhagwan Krishna does not automatically know everything just by being where he is — things are still brought and reported to him, because (per this teaching) "obviously , he has more contacts" than others.

3. Why even Bholenath and Hanuman ji Maharaj ar e said to still need "service"/communication: Per this teaching, the reason so many people worship and serve Bholenath (Bhagwan Shiva) and Hanuman ji Maharaj is that they too have that many "doots" (messengers/emissaries) reporting to them — even they need connection and communication rather than knowing everything unaided.

4. A trikaldarshi (one who can per ceive past, pr esent, and futur e) does not use that ability to look at just anything: Per this teaching, someone who genuinely possesses trikaldarshi ability is described as never simply "looking" at things through it on their own initiative or for casual curiosity .

5. The body as a "device" that can only be opened, not a sour ce of knowledge in itself: Per this teaching, a person's own body/senses function like a device that can only be "opened" — much as opening the ears lets a person hear , or opening one's drishti (inner sight) lets a person see — but showing and telling what appears still requires someone else on the other end; a person cannot generate this knowledge purely "by themselves."

6. "Aham Brahmasmi" is r eframed, per this teaching, as a caution rather than a literal claim: Per this teaching, the realization that "I am Brahm" is corrected here to mean the opposite in a practical sense — "you are not [Brahm]"; what a person can actually do is open their own body/vessel to receive, not generate divine knowledge from themselves; per this teaching, a person's own uplift (uddhar) genuinely begins at the point they understand this distinction.

7. Manifestation claims ar e gently corr ected, per this teaching: Per this teaching, a person who claims "I will manifest it myself" is told their manifestation "is nothing" on its own — what a person can actually do is pray , and the power that then acts comes from above; the recommended posture is to stay content and at ease ("mauj mein raho") rather than straining to manifest through personal willpower .
Part B — Samarpan (Surr ender) as What Actually Determines Whether Drishti Is Accurate

1. Why "samarpan" (surr ender) is emphasized in bhakti, per this teaching: Per this teaching, saying "Baba, you do it" in genuine surrender is what allows another power to come and act on a devotee's behalf, which is why a person of complete trust/faith ("vishwaas") is described as having their wishes fulfilled almost as a matter of course.

2. Ordinary people without special drishti ar e said to still per ceive corr ectly in ordinary matters: Per this teaching, devotees without any special inner sight (illustrated with "Anu" and "V ikas bhaiya," who are described as not having drishti) are still described as perceiving things correctly in the ordinary sense; the speaker states his real concern is specifically for those WHO DO have drishti — "what happened to them" — implying that special inner sight brings its own particular challenges.
3. "Our work is pr ecisely third-eye activation": Per this teaching, the speaker states directly that helping devotees activate their third eye/inner sight is the core work being done.

4. Why incr eased visibility of the unseen can cr eate new pr oblems: Per this teaching, once a devotee's inner "screen" is invoked and things genuinely start becoming visible, the mind ("dimaag") can start running alongside what is seen and interfering with it — producing uncertainty about whether a given impression is a genuine perception or the mind's own invention, and a great deal of second-guessing ("papa is telling something else and I'm thinking something else").

5. Why samarpan, not raw effort, is what r esolves this uncertainty: Per this teaching, this uncertainty resolves in favor of someone who is completely surrendered — "the more surrender you have, the more correctly it will start appearing to you" — which is why the speaker states he has, over time, shifted his own teaching emphasis away from gyaan (knowledge/technique) and increasingly toward samarpan.

6. A caution against over confidence once vision does become r eliable: Per this teaching, as a devotee's samarpan grows and their inner vision starts appearing correctly , this is watched carefully — the moment it starts appearing "too well," the devotee is deliberately called back/checked, implying a built-in safeguard against ego or overreach once real accuracy develops.

7. Effort alone, without samarpan, is described as insufficient: Per this teaching, even a devotee who works extremely hard — described as possibly the hardest-working devotee of all — cannot substitute pure ef fort for samarpan; per this teaching, no
power comes chasing after someone on the strength of ef fort or yogic technique alone, without the accompanying element of surrender .
Part C — Illustrative Cases: Shrikant Bhaiya, the Devotee Who Over came Doshas, and Shivram Bhaiya

1. "Shrikant bhaiya" as an example of samarpan r eaching an advanced ("ultra") level: Per this teaching, a devotee referred to as Shrikant bhaiya is described as having reached a very advanced level of perception; his own daily commitment is limited to two hours of sitting/practice, with the rest surrendered entirely to Baba — and per this teaching, whatever he decides (even in ordinary contexts like his own of fice) tends to come to pass, illustrated as a direct result of that combination of consistent practice and complete surrender rather than additional personal striving.

2. "Pre-work" can feel harder than the task itself once begun: Per this teaching, the anticipation or preparation before doing something can feel more dif ficult than actually doing it — once a devotee begins, things are described as flowing in rapidly ("dhadaadhad dhadaadhad aane lagta hai").

3. Even sparse initial impr essions can turn out to be fully accurate: Per this teaching, a devotee's perception may initially feel like only a few fragments ("only four lines") are visible, yet when reported, those fragments turn out to be exactly , precisely correct — illustrating that accuracy is not necessarily proportional to how much detail is initially perceived.

4. A devotee r eferred to as "Anshu" is described as struggling mor e visibly with this pr ocess: Per this teaching, this devotee is described as frequently reporting that she "can't see anything," making her (along with one other devotee) a frequent subject of feedback/review on this front.

5. A devotee once carrying doshas (afflictions) that blocked their own efforts is described as now r eceiving the most grace: Per this teaching (kept general here per this teaching's own privacy practice), a devotee who at one point could not accomplish tasks on their own — burdened with doshas connected to matters of "cutting bandhan" (severing bonds, connecting back to this project's earlier teaching on kriya-cutting) — was, per this teaching, the very first person the speaker examined; today , this same devotee is described as receiving an especially strong degree of grace from Baba across financial, physical, and family matters, now living in a way described as distinctly set apart from ordinary patterns.

6. The instruction not to abandon one's own sense of self after such transformation: Per this teaching, once a devotee reaches a state of unusual grace or ability , they are cautioned not to lose their own grounded sense of identity — illustrated with a devotee referred to as "Shivram bhaiya," described with the epithet "surya tej" (sun-radiance), where questions like whether he currently holds an ordinary job are treated as beside the point.

7. What this teaching offers to devotees without that same level of attainment: Per this teaching, devotees who do not have that same "surya tej" are told that ordinary devotion and prayer to God remains fully their own path; per this teaching, someone who continues praying even after already having everything they materially need is described as being "made for something bigger" — with the scale of a person's eventual task determining the scale of the training required to prepare them for it.
Part D — How the Guru Deliberately Withholds Answers to Build a Disciple's Own Drishti

1. Why the speaker deliberately avoids dir ectly confirming things a devotee alr eady senses: Per this teaching, the speaker explains that he deliberately avoids directly telling a devotee things they are on the ver ge of perceiving themselves — reasoning that if he confirms it outright, the devotee will start overthinking it and grow impatient/"hyperactive" asking why it hasn't happened yet — even though he knows that whatever he would say will, within roughly the next ten days, appear directly in that devotee's own drishti regardless.

2. The moment that marks a devotee's own drishti/connection genuinely opening: Per this teaching, when a devotee begins saying things they themselves never read or heard before, or is able to state someone's name sitting right there with no ordinary way of knowing it, that is the sign to trust that Gurudev has begun speaking through them, that shakti has arrived, and that guru's kripa (grace) has been received — and, per this teaching, the very first realization that comes with this is understanding that "we don't actually know anything ourselves," since the accurate information came from elsewhere, not from the devotee's own mind.

3. Why sharing such per ceptions with the guru is still worthwhile, per this teaching: Per this teaching, a devotee reporting what they perceive to the guru, rather than keeping it to themselves, is described as what allows the process to work fully; per this teaching, a devotee who has mantra shakti but lacks trust/faith in it does not benefit fully from it, while a devotee who has both trust and mantra shakti together is protected such that "nobody can touch a hair on them," and their ef forts come to fruition.

4. Why gr eat saints and mahatmas ar e ultimately described as always r eturning to the theme of surr ender: Per this teaching, this is of fered as the underlying reason accomplished spiritual figures consistently emphasize samarpan above all else, even after teaching every technique they know — because technique alone, without the devotee actually beginning to perceive for themselves, cannot be taken further .
Part E — Real Shakti Comes Only Fr om the Awakened "T elling" Vision, Never From Claimed On-Demand Fortune-T elling

1. Why the ordinary mind cannot corr ectly pictur e what has genuinely been "set up" for someone: Per this teaching, if the speaker tells a listener that something has been "set up behind" a particular devotee, the listener's own ordinary mind will inevitably picture something mundane and likely wrong, because they are imagining it through their own conceptual lens rather than perceiving it directly — the same applies if told a "gift" has been sent to someone: the mind will picture an ordinary gift rather than the real thing.

2. Where real shakti actually comes fr om, per this teaching: Per this teaching, the shakti most devotees are actively seeking comes specifically from this awakened "telling" vision — not from casually discussing or imagining it in the ordinary sense; genuine validation, per this teaching, happens only when the perception presents itself directly and unmistakably (illustrated as someone unknown walking up, addressing a person by name unprompted, and bowing to them, having never been told to do so by anyone).

3. A clear warning against claiming casual, on-demand fortune-telling: Per this teaching, claiming to be able to simply "look at someone's path (future) and tell them" on request is described as something a person genuinely cannot do; what a devotee can actually do is observe activity and act according to their own accumulated experience — nothing more casual or ondemand than that.

4. Starting fr om a genuinely "empty vessel" for real clarity: Per this teaching, someone seeking a deeper level of clarity is advised to let go of everything and start completely from zero, since only a truly empty vessel hears clearly .

5. Why the guru deliberately withholds answers fr om frustrated devotees: Per this teaching, when devotees grow frustrated and press to "just ask Baba," the speaker deliberately does not always answer — illustrated with a devotee ("Anshu") who is said to ask roughly 200 questions, of which only around 70 receive an answer , specifically because only those 70 have come through with real clarity; the rest are deliberately left unanswered rather than answered incorrectly , even though this sometimes draws the complaint that "bhaiya didn't answer ."
Part F — Burning Kriya, Receptors, and Tap Shakti

1. What "burning kriya" is, per this teaching: A tantrik captures a tar get's subtle body (sookshm sharir), properly consecrates and installs life-force into the captured item (an imperfect installation is itself unstable), binds it, and burns it in the practitioner's own inner fire (agni) — not the ordinary visible fire, but the practitioner's own accumulated fire; if this genuinely succeeds, the tar get may not wake the next morning, appearing to doctors as an unexplained internal collapse with skin marks, since they burn away internally by evening.

2. Why the visible fir e itself is not what matters: The physical-world fire you can see is not the same as astral-world fire, which produces a dif ferent kind of ener gy; a burning kriya works either through ordinary physical fire (which must be sustained, not a brief flare) or through the practitioner's own tap shakti (accumulated spiritual heat/power) — and a tar get whose own body's tap shakti already exceeds the level the attacker can produce simply will not burn, regardless of how much fire is directed at them.

3. Tap shakti in saints, and how it is built: A genuine saint's body is said to carry so much accumulated fire that a single utterance of their name produces ener gy equivalent to thousands of havans; an ordinary devotee can grow their own tap shakti without limit through sustained, regular mantra japa.

4. The "receptor" concept, and why cr ossing r oughly 4 cr or e japa r emoves it: A "receptor" is described as the specific point through which anything from the astral world can contact/communicate with a person (analogous to recognizing your own name being called). Per this teaching, once a devotee crosses roughly 4 crore (40 million) total japa, Hanuman ji Maharaj removes this receptor entirely — after which no tantra-mantra-yantra kriya can be performed on that person at all, since there is no longer any receiving end for it to connect to.

5. How consistent japa turns the body into a "walking havan kund": Just four minutes of japa is described as bringing enough fire into the body that a devotee ef fectively becomes a mobile, continuously burning fire-altar; this specific technique was taught to the speaker by Hanuman ji Maharaj roughly two and a half years before this recording and has been practiced regularly since. Physical havan participation reinforces the same ef fect: during a havan performed with genuine sankalp, a devotee's own subtle body sits near the fire and is "cooked"/strengthened in proportion to the ahutis (of ferings) made.

6. The speaker's own personal tap-shakti account: The speaker states he has personally given roughly 70 lakh (7 million) ahutis to date (one ahuti corresponding to every ten mantras of japa, so roughly 70 crore/700 million japa), separate from mahavan totals, and prays specifically that his own havan practice never stop, even at the cost of his own body; as of this recording, roughly 534 devotees are said to be doing japa while treating the speaker as their sakshi (witness), and each such devotee's own tap shakti grows proportionally through that act.
Part G — The Two Causes of Spiritual Downfall (Patan)

1. The first cause — one's own accumulated fir e becoming ego and consuming the practitioner: Illustrated with a devotee ("Harshvardhan") deep in agni-tattva sadhna, and with the traditional account of Sati Mata self-immolating through her own tap shakti (ordinary fire being too weak to burn her) — a person who reaches an advanced level of accumulated fire can, if that fire turns into ahankar (ego), be consumed by their own attainment; this is described as a purely self-inflicted cause of downfall, not caused by anything external.

2. The second, mor e common cause — holding shakti without "Shiv" (the sanctioned sour ce/method): As a devotee's grahan shakti (receiving capacity) grows, Bhagwan Shiv is described as providing a correspondingly lar ger "bowl" to hold it; per this teaching, downfall most commonly comes from switching one's method, guru, or lineage without proper sanction — shakti received or held this way , disconnected from its proper sanctioned source, is described as eventually turning destructive ("shakti tandav karti hai").

3. The illustrative corr ection — never try to bypass the sanctioned guru channel: A devotee ("Manav") who was told by someone outside the community that he could skip "Bhaiya" (the guru figure, referred to here by his own name, Parikshit, as part of the teaching) and approach Hanuman ji Maharaj directly is firmly corrected: per this teaching, Hanuman ji Maharaj

would refuse such a person and send them away , since loyalty to the sanctioned channel is a precondition for that connection — any name may be substituted for the example used, the general principle being that a devotee cannot bypass their sanctioned guru-lineage and expect direct acceptance elsewhere.

4. Once a guru is accepted, the r elationship is tr eated as absolute: Per this teaching, a devotee's own foundational devotion (their kul devata, their original sanctioned method) should never be abandoned; a devotee who abandons their "mool" (root/origin) is said to end up with nothing, a pattern the speaker describes as visible throughout history . A guru mantra received through a sanctioned lineage can coexist with reverence for other , greater figures (for example, Hanuman ji Maharaj) as long as it is done "with the reference of," i.e. under the sanction of, the original guru — it is specifically abandoning or bypassing that sanctioned relationship altogether that is discouraged.
Part H — The Vayus, and the Guru's Safer Udaan-V ayu Technique

1. The body's vayus (subtle air currents), per this teaching: Samaan vayu operates in the upper -middle body , apaan vayu in the lower body , udaan vayu below the navel and moving upward, and praan vayu pervades every particle throughout and around the body; when udaan vayu moves upward with strength, it acts directly on the praan tattva.

2. Why dir ectly activating praan vayu (as some yogic techniques attempt) is risky: Some practitioners have historically tried to activate praan tattva directly — through techniques like bhastrika (rapid breath-pumping) or various bandhas (bodily locks) — sometimes calling the resulting sur ge "kundalini shakti"; per this teaching, this ef fect is directly proportional to praan vayu, and directly manipulating praan vayu this way carries real risk, since it can significantly lengthen or shorten a person's lifespan depending on how it is handled — tradition is cited as counting a person's allotted lifespan in breaths, not days or years, with each breath carrying one unit of universal praan-tattva ener gy .

3. The yogic br eath-spending appr oach versus the samadhi br eath-conserving appr oach: Rapid, sustained breath techniques (illustrated with a well-known yoga teacher doing continuous bhastrika) intentionally "spend" many breaths quickly to gather praan urja into the body for healing — an approach this teaching connects (in a dif ferent sense) to a concept found in the Patanjali Yoga Sutras — but since ener gy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted, increasing body-ener gy this way is understood to draw down some other resource (illustratively , the lifespan/breath allotment). By contrast, a yogi in samadhi (illustrated with devotees "Anshu" and "Rohit bhaiya," who are described as entering samadhi at Ashaeiynn) slows their breathing dramatically while remaining fully conscious, conserving breath (and praan ener gy) rather than spending it — described as the deeper , intended aim behind the Patanjali framework.

4. Why bringing udaan vayu straight upward (the common traditional appr oach) is unr eliable and risky: Many traditions teach bringing udaan vayu straight up to the head to awaken all the chakras at once; per this teaching, this is extremely dif ficult, makes the practitioner an immediate tar get ("the astral world will eat you"), and is not guaranteed to hold even if achieved — it can recede back down afterward.

5. The guru's alternative technique — storing the energy rather than for cing it upward: Instead of pushing udaan-vayugenerated ener gy directly upward, the guru taught storing it via sankalp in a specific realm/vessel, continuously regenerating and redirecting it into storage this way rather than exposing it directly; this was combined with a controlled-pain method learned from a hatha-yogi ascetic, paralleling (but distinct from) the physical austerities naga sadhus and brahmacharis practice at events like the Kumbh Mela specifically to prevent desire (vaasna) from arising, since desire and worship ("upasana") are described as running together and interfering with one another as this ener gy increases.

6. The 21-mahavan pr ocess for safely absorbing this energy: Because udaan vayu's ener gy is inherently intense/uncontrollable, it is blended with "Ram tattvas" and distributed gradually across a structured 21-mahavan series rather than all at once, so devotees can safely absorb and hold manifold increases in body ener gy , personal capability , and attraction/personality power; because this ener gy touches every area of daily life, participating devotees are told to take a little extra care, with the guru

committing (via two personal sankalps) to maintain full protective cover throughout the process. Mahavan participation fees are kept at half the standard rate or less, per the guru's own guru's instruction, with anything additional treated as a voluntary donation only .
Part I — Why Consistent Devotees Rar ely Face New Threats: The "Hostel Territory" Analogy

1. The hostel analogy for how pr etas (spirits) operate: Just as hostel seniors initially harass a newcomer with petty pranks until the newcomer becomes used to it (and may eventually be feared themselves), pretas in the astral world operate the same way — a person's consistent daily routine and fixed locations expose them only to a small, familiar , "territorial" set of pretas, similar to how humans and even dogs have their own territories that others don't casually cross into; per this teaching, this means a fixed routine does not expose a devotee to broader astral risk than moving around would.

2. What happens as a devotee's japa gr ows str onger: The small set of local pretas that used to bother a devotee eventually find they "can't handle it anymore" and may call in outside reinforcement, paralleling how a hostel dispute might escalate by calling in outside friends — but per this teaching, consistent daily japa performed with genuine "sakshi bhaav" (treating the guru/deity as active witness) provides real-time protection during the practice itself, to the point that not even a deva shakti will interrupt a devotee actively engaged in japa this way .
Part J — Jhapatte, Third-Eye Focus Warnings, and Kul Devata/Pitru Dosha

1. Why vulnerability incr eases right after finishing practice, and why "jhapatte" (jolts) fade over time: A devotee is described as more vulnerable to ener gy fluctuations for a period immediately after concluding japa and releasing their sankalp — sometimes producing peace, sometimes irritability . These occasional jhapatte (sudden jolts) gradually diminish and eventually stop as protective "layers" build up in the body through consistent practice; occasional lar ger jhapatte can still occur , but doing even five minutes more of japa restores balance — which is why consistent daily practice (even if brief) matters more than occasional long sessions.

2. A direct warning against for cing focus specifically on the third-eye point: Per this teaching, excessive, forced focus on making something appear specifically at the third-eye location can actually "burn"/overload a devotee's drishti; genuine perception comes simply from closing the eyes in ordinary meditative practice, not from straining to focus on a specific point. A devotee whose drishti gets burned this way experiences a few days of complete blankness while "mantra doots" (mantra messengers) work to restore it, typically over one to three days.

3. Kul devata (family deity) and pitru (ancestor) dosha as a distinct block on drishti: Until a devotee's kul devata is fully satisfied with them, ancestral pitru connected to that family line will continue interfering and holding back spiritual progress, regardless of how much the devotee personally practices; a kul devata connection cannot be properly established without a guru, since a guru provides the necessary authorization for it. Illustrated with devotees "Anshu" and her sister "Shalini" ("Shalu"), whose family's kul devi was initially very displeased but, through sustained devotional practice, is now described as standing closely behind both sisters — with Anshu specifically able to enter samadhi within about five minutes of starting japa.

4. A prescribed remedy for a devotee who feels blocked despite corr ect practice: Light an akhand deepak (continuouslyburning lamp) for 1 1 days dedicated to the kul devata, of fered the same way a lamp is of fered to Hanuman ji Maharaj, along with a prayer asking the kul devata to intervene with any troublesome pitru, to for give any mistakes, and to allow devotion to progress; a devotee's regular japa can also be dedicated to the kul devata at its conclusion the same way it is normally dedicated to Hanuman ji Maharaj as sakshi — no separate name is required, since "Ram's name applies equally ."

5. A dosha fr om a shraap (curse) r equires roughly elevenfold effort for a period, not permanent extra work: A dosha is described as always originating from a real curse, and such doshas do not resolve quickly on their own — they must be actively

"cut" through sustained ef fort. A devotee carrying such a dosha needs roughly eleven times the ordinary ef fort for some finite period; per this teaching, most people who quit early (after a couple of days without results) do so because no one told them this specific extra ef fort was required and time-limited, leading them to wander between teachers and blame the method rather than recognizing their own unaddressed dosha.

6. A resolved illustrative case, and its contrast: A devotee (implicitly Anshu, from the earlier illustration), previously extremely restless and full of doubts when she first arrived, stuck with consistent practice — aided by her mother and sister physically pulling her back to it during dif ficult periods — and eventually reached the advanced state described earlier; her sister Shalu, more naturally patient, simply followed instructions from the start.

7. A "devta-tulya" (deity-equivalent) pitru as a fifth possible cause, and its own complication: If a family ancestor genuinely attained real siddhi through their own sadhna in life, they can become a benevolent, powerful guardian pitru who never troubles descendants and instead channels sustained material fortune to the family across generations. However , because such a powerful pitru itself receives ongoing devotional of ferings from the family , it can act with more autonomy — a family member who doubts or resists such a pitru (while everyone else in the family reveres it) is described as tending to suf fer the worst of anyone in that family as a result, since the pitru holds vastly more power than an ordinary person can counter .

8. The remedy for this fifth cause: Increasing one's own mantra shakti to a level that surpasses the powerful ancestral pitru's own ener gy — once a devotee's tap/mantra shakti exceeds that level, the pitru can no longer even approach them (would itself be harmed on contact), echoing why pretas cannot approach genuine saints or enter a temple where a deity is truly present.
Part K — Milestones on the Path: Fr om 4 Cr or e to 14 Cr or e Japa

1. The Gorakhnath story — accumulated tap shakti so str ong it pr events even a deity fr om manifesting: Per this teaching (presented as a true account), one of two brothers received darshan of the Lord within two months of starting sadhna; the other did not, and after eight years of unrewarded Mahamrityunjaya mantra japa, quit for six months out of frustration. Given a dif ferent mantra by a devotee of Baba Gorakhnath, he began hearing an unfamiliar voice within three days of starting it in a cave; when asked to appear , the voice (identifying itself as Gorakhnath) explained it could not manifest visibly , because the tap accumulated through his years of Mahamrityunjaya practice would itself burn/harm the deity on contact — illustrating that a devotee whose practice seems to have "failed" to produce visible results may in fact have accumulated very significant protective tap shakti.

2. Why sustained mantra shakti, not visible drishti, is the r eal marker of pr ogr ess: Per this teaching, chasing visible perception (drishti) as the primary sign of progress is a mistake; sustained, high-volume mantra shakti ("mantra sarkar") is presented as the truly decisive protective factor , regardless of how much a devotee can currently "see."

3. The 4-cr or e threshold: Below roughly 4 crore (40 million) total japa, any early claims of an "opened" drishti (illustrated with devotees claiming results after only about 14 lakh/1.4 million japa) are described as inherently unstable. 4 crore is presented as the baseline threshold for genuine purification — before which no devotee should claim any ability to help or act on others' behalf. Between roughly 1-2 crore, some devotees may find japa continuing somewhat automatically even during daily activity; by 4 crore, this becomes fully continuous "on the move," and a genuine, ongoing flow of spiritual connection/power is described as beginning at that point.

4. The 14-cr or e threshold: Per what the speaker's own guru/Hanuman ji Maharaj reportedly told him, at 14 crore japa all of a devotee's doshas and papas — even something as serious as a brahm hatya (killing a Brahmin) dosha, if present — are said to be fully cut away , at which point the devotee attains direct darshan of God and the capability for direct two-way communication, with suf ficiently good karma potentially allowing full, unmistakable divine manifestation.
